Cytogenetics

Updated Oct 8, 2026 Revision 1.0 6 learning objectives

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Describe what a normal chromosome is made of, how it is identified, and why chromosome analysis is used clinically.
  2. LO 2Compare mitosis and meiosis, and predict the chromosomes that result when either goes wrong.
  3. LO 3Recognize the common abnormalities in the number of autosomes and sex chromosomes.
  4. LO 4Name the kinds of structural chromosome changes and what each does to offspring.
  5. LO 5Define chromosomal mosaicism and explain how it arises.
  6. LO 6Explain confined placental mosaicism and why it matters for prenatal testing.

MAPBig-picture map of chromosome abnormalities

LO 1Normal chromosomes

Q1. What is a normal human chromosome set?
  • 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY)
  • ≈20,000 genes spread over 400–1,000 visible bands → one band ≠ one gene; each band holds hundreds of genes
Trap

A visible band is a large stretch of DNA. A deletion of one band removes many genes, which is why even "small" visible deletions cause syndromes.

Q2. What are the parts of a chromosome?
TelomereCentromere
WhereCaps the ends of each armPrimary constriction between p and q
JobSeals chromatin; prevents fusion with other chromosomesSite where the spindle attaches and pulls chromatids to opposite poles
SequenceAlways TTAGGG, repeated hundreds to thousands of timesHighly repetitive, but unique to each chromosome
EuchromatinHeterochromatin
PackingLess condensedMore condensed
DNACoding (active genes)Mostly noncoding
WhereChromosome armsAround centromeres and the distal Y
Memory tool

p = petite (short arm); q comes next in the alphabet (long arm). Euchromatin = "truly" active; heterochromatin = "different," packed away.

Step 1

Acrocentric chromosomes (centromere near one end, tiny p arms): 13, 14, 15, 21, 22. Only these form Robertsonian translocations. Telomerase keeps telomeres long in stem and cancer cells.

Q3. How are chromosomes analyzed, and when is it used?
  • Analysis uses cells in metaphase, when chromosomes are most condensed and line up
  • Cells are grown, arrested in metaphase, spread and G-banded → karyotype
  • Meiotic cells are extremely hard to prepare, so meiosis is studied indirectly
  • Standard G-banding misses changes under ≈5 Mb; use high-resolution banding, FISH or chromosomal microarray
Clinical useExample
Suspected aneuploidyDown, Turner, Klinefelter features
Malformations / developmental delayUnexplained birth defects
Reproductive problemsRecurrent miscarriage, infertility (look for balanced translocations)
Prenatal testingCVS, amniocentesis
CancerLeukemia translocations
In-house exam

Know why chromosomes are studied at metaphase and why meiotic chromosomes are rarely studied directly.

Q4. What do the terms and karyotype notation mean?

Numerical

  • Haploid = n (23)
  • Triploid = 3n (69)
  • Tetraploid = 4n (92)
  • Aneuploid: trisomy 2n+1; monosomy 2n−1

Structural

  • Deletion = partial monosomy
  • Duplication = partial trisomy
  • Also translocation, inversion, ring, isochromosome
KaryotypeMeaning
47,XY,+21Male with trisomy 21
45,XTurner syndrome
46/47,+21Mosaic: normal and trisomy 21 cell lines
45,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10)Balanced Robertsonian 14;21 carrier (45 chromosomes)
46,XX,t(7;21)(q21;q11.2)Balanced reciprocal translocation carrier
46,XY,der(21)t(7;21)(q21;q11.2)Unbalanced: inherited only the derivative 21

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1Why can't a single G-band deletion be described as a single-gene disorder?
There are ≈20,000 genes over only 400–1,000 bands, so each band holds many genes; losing one removes many.
A2A child has features of a microdeletion syndrome but a normal G-banded karyotype. Next test?
Chromosomal microarray or FISH: microdeletions are usually <5 Mb and missed by G-banding.

LO 2Mitosis, meiosis and nondisjunction

Q1. What happens in mitosis?

Purpose: make identical, diploid daughter cells for growth and replacing dying cells.

PhaseKey event
Interphase (G1, S, G2)Growth; DNA copied in S phase
ProphaseChromosomes condense; spindle and centrioles form
PrometaphaseNuclear membrane disappears
MetaphaseChromosomes line up on the metaphase plate (stage used for analysis)
AnaphaseCentromeres divide; sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles
TelophaseCytokinesis; nuclear membrane reforms; chromosomes decondense
Memory tool

PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase (Middle), Anaphase (Apart), Telophase (Two). Prometaphase sits between P and M.

Q2. What happens in meiosis, and why are there two divisions?

Occurs in germ cells only. Purpose: make haploid eggs and sperm with new gene combinations through independent assortment and recombination.

StageWhat happensChromosomes per cell
StartDNA replicated46, each with 2 chromatids
Meiosis IHomologs pair; recombination in prophase I (synaptonemal complex, crossing over); independent assortment; homologs separate = reduction division23, each with 2 chromatids
Meiosis IILike mitosis: sister chromatids separate23, each with 1 chromatid

One crossover produces two parental-type and two recombinant gametes.

High yield

Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Every nondisjunction question depends on this.

Q3. How does meiosis differ in males and females?
MalesFemales
ProductsAll 4 become sperm1 mature oocyte + 2 polar bodies
CytoplasmDivided evenlyDivided unequally
StartsPuberty, after many mitotic divisionsFetal life, after fewer mitotic divisions
TimingContinuous, done in weeksArrested in prophase I before birth; resumes each cycle at ovulation; arrests in metaphase II; completed only after fertilization
Analogy — the paused movie

Each oocyte is a movie paused at the same scene (prophase I) for 12–45 years. The longer the pause, the more likely the chromosomes come apart wrongly when "play" is pressed. That is why nondisjunction rises with maternal age.

Q4. How do mitosis and meiosis compare overall?
Meiosis ("reduce")Mitosis ("split")
Two divisionsOne division
Germ cellsSomatic cells
Homologous chromosomes pairHomologs act independently
Daughter cells haploidDaughter cells diploid
Daughter cells have new assortments of parental chromosomesIdentical daughter cells
Q5. What happens when chromosomes fail to separate (nondisjunction)?

Nondisjunction = failure of chromosomes to separate. It is the mechanism of aneuploidy and happens most often in meiosis I of oogenesis.

Meiosis I errorMeiosis II error
What failsHomologs don't separateSister chromatids don't separate
GametesAll 4 abnormal: 2 with both homologs (n+1), 2 with none (n−1)2 normal, 1 with two identical copies (n+1), 1 with none (n−1)
After fertilizationTrisomy or monosomyNormal, trisomy or monosomy
Step 1

A meiosis I error gives a gamete with both different homologs (heterodisomy); a meiosis II error gives two identical copies (isodisomy). If the zygote later loses the extra copy ("trisomy rescue"), it can be left with uniparental disomy (both copies from one parent), a cause of Prader-Willi syndrome.

In-house exam

Be able to draw nondisjunction in MI vs MII and state the gametes from each.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A nondisjunction leaves half of the gametes normal. Which division failed?
Meiosis II. A meiosis I error makes all four gametes abnormal.
A2Why are female eggs more prone to nondisjunction than sperm?
Oocytes are arrested in prophase I from fetal life until ovulation, years to decades later; risk rises with maternal age.

LO 3Numerical abnormalities

Q1. How common is aneuploidy, and which kinds survive?
  • Most common and clinically significant chromosome disorder: >3–4% of recognized pregnancies
  • Trisomy can occur for any chromosome but is rarely viable (21, 18, 13 and sex chromosomes are the survivors)
  • Monosomy of a whole chromosome is always lethal, except monosomy X
  • Mechanism: nondisjunction, most often maternal meiosis I
High yield

The only viable full monosomy is 45,X (Turner).

Q2. What do autosomal abnormalities have in common?
  1. Developmental delay / intellectual disability
  2. Facial features that look more like others with the syndrome than like family members
  3. Growth delay
  4. Congenital malformations
Q3. How do the three viable autosomal trisomies compare?
Trisomy 21 (Down)Trisomy 18 (Edwards)Trisomy 13 (Patau)
Face / bodyLow nasal root, upslanting palpebral fissures, round cheeks, downturned mouth, short neck, flat occiputPrenatal growth deficiency; clenched hands with overlapping fingers, small jaw, prominent occiputMidline defects: oral clefts, spina bifida, omphalocele; microphthalmia
Heart40% congenital heart defectCongenital heart defects (VSD)Congenital heart defects
Other15–20× ↑ leukemia risk——
IntellectModerate–severe disabilityProfoundProfound
SurvivalInto adulthood95% miscarried; 50% die in first weeks; 5% reach 1 year95% miscarried; 5% of those born reach 1 year

Trisomy 21

  • Upslanting fissures, flat face, low nasal root

Trisomy 18

  • Clenched hands, overlapping fingers, growth deficiency

Trisomy 13

  • Cleft lip/palate, small eyes, polydactyly
Memory tool

Match the number to a milestone age: Drinking age 21 (Down), Election (voting) age 18 (Edwards), Puberty at 13 (Patau). D-E-P in order of decreasing number.

In-house exam

Down syndrome causes: ≈95% meiotic nondisjunction (maternal age), ≈4% Robertsonian translocation (higher recurrence if a parent carries it), ≈2% mosaicism (milder).

Step 1
  • Down: AV septal defect (endocardial cushion), duodenal atresia ("double bubble"), Hirschsprung, single palmar crease, sandal gap, early-onset Alzheimer (APP on chr 21), ALL and AML (megakaryoblastic); 1st-trimester ↑ nuchal translucency, ↓ PAPP-A, ↑ hCG; quad screen ↓ AFP, ↑ hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin A.
  • Edwards: rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, micrognathia; quad screen ↓ AFP, ↓ hCG, ↓ estriol, normal/↓ inhibin.
  • Patau: holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, cutis aplasia, microphthalmia; ↓ PAPP-A, ↓ hCG.
Q4. Why are sex chromosome abnormalities milder than autosomal ones?
  1. The Y has few active genes (<50), mostly for gonadal and genital development
  2. X inactivation (Lyon hypothesis): when more than one X is present, all but one are inactivated early in development and seen as Barr bodies. Which X is silenced is random in each early cell, so females are naturally mosaic
Step 1

Number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1. 47,XXY has one Barr body; 45,X has none.

Q5. What are the main sex chromosome syndromes?
TurnerKlinefelter47,XXX47,XYY
KaryotypeMost often 45,XMost often 47,XXY47,XXX47,XYY
HeightShort (proportionate)Tall, disproportionately long limbsTaller than averageTaller than average
GonadsOvarian dysgenesis, sexual infantilismSmall testes, sterile (seminiferous tubule atrophy)Premature ovarian failureUsually normal
OtherWebbed neck, low hairline, broad shield chest, congenital heart defectsGynecomastia in ⅓; IQ 10–15 points below siblingsLower IQ than sibsHyperactivity, ADD, learning disabilities; lower IQ than sibs
Overall——Relatively benign; usually chromosomally normal offspring

Turner (45,X)

  • Short, broad shield chest, sexual infantilism

Klinefelter (47,XXY)

  • Tall, long limbs, gynecomastia, small testes
Step 1
  • Turner: most common cause of primary amenorrhea; bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, horseshoe kidney, lymphedema / cystic hygroma at birth; streak ovaries → ↓ estrogen, ↑ FSH/LH. Often arises from loss of the paternal X; not maternal-age related.
  • Klinefelter: hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (↓ testosterone, ↑ FSH/LH, ↓ inhibin, ↑ estrogen); most common chromosomal cause of male infertility.

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A newborn with clenched fists, overlapping fingers and a VSD. Most likely karyotype and outlook?
47,+18 (Edwards); ≈5% survive to 1 year.
A2A tall 17-year-old boy with small firm testes, gynecomastia and learning difficulties. Karyotype and Barr bodies?
47,XXY (Klinefelter) with one Barr body.
A3Why can a woman with 47,XXX look nearly normal while trisomy 18 is lethal?
Extra X chromosomes are inactivated (Barr bodies), limiting the extra gene dose; autosomes have no such mechanism.

LO 4Structural abnormalities

Q1. What is a Robertsonian translocation?
  • Whole-arm exchange between two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22)
  • Breaks occur in the short arms; the two long arms fuse at the centromere; the short arms (no essential genes, repeated elsewhere) are lost
  • Most common: t(13;14)
  • Balanced carrier: 45 chromosomes (healthy). Unbalanced: 46 chromosomes (extra long arm = translocation trisomy)
  • Carrier females pass on unbalanced forms more often than carrier males
  • ≈4% of Down syndrome is from a Robertsonian translocation

Formation

  • Short arms break off; long arms join

Balanced vs unbalanced

  • Balanced: 45 chromosomes, normal gene dose
  • Unbalanced: 46 chromosomes, three copies of 21q
Trap

A Down syndrome child with 46 chromosomes has a translocation, not standard trisomy. Test the parents: if one is a balanced carrier (45 chromosomes), the recurrence risk is far higher than the age-based risk.

Step 1

A carrier of der(21;21) (Robertsonian between the two 21s) can only produce trisomy 21 or monosomy 21 conceptions: 100% of live births have Down syndrome.

Q2. What is a reciprocal translocation, and what happens to the carrier's children?
  • Exchange of segments between two (usually nonhomologous) chromosomes; any translocation that is not Robertsonian
  • Mostly family-specific, not recurrent
  • Balanced: 46 chromosomes; ≈70% inherited. Unbalanced: 46 (rarely 47)
  • In meiosis, the four chromosomes pair as a cross-shaped quadrivalent
SegregationGametes
AlternateOne normal + one balanced (all genes present, just swapped)
Adjacent-1Two unbalanced: partial trisomy of one segment + partial monosomy of the other
Adjacent-2Unbalanced (less common)

Phenotype of the unbalanced child depends on the size of the unbalanced segment, the genes involved, and whether the imbalance is mainly monosomic (worse) or trisomic.

In-house exam

Example: mother 46,XX,t(7;21)(q21;q11.2) (balanced) → fetus 46,XY,der(21)t(7;21)(q21;q11.2) (unbalanced: partial trisomy 7q + partial monosomy 21q). A chromosome count alone can't tell balanced from unbalanced reciprocal translocations: both are 46.

Step 1

Balanced translocation carriers present with recurrent miscarriage or infertility. Acquired reciprocal translocations drive cancers: t(9;22) CML, t(15;17) APL, t(8;14) Burkitt, t(14;18) follicular lymphoma.

Q3. What kinds of deletions are there?
TypeBreaksResult
Terminal1Loss of a chromosome end
Interstitial2Loss of a middle segment
Ring2Both ends (and telomeres) lost; broken ends fuse into a ring with the centromere

Microdeletions

  • Usually <5 Mb → can be missed by G-banding
  • Seen with high-resolution chromosomes (sometimes), FISH, or chromosomal microarray
  • Example: DiGeorge / velocardiofacial syndrome (22q11.2)
Step 1
  • 22q11.2 (DiGeorge): CATCH-22: cleft palate, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia (T-cell deficiency), cardiac (conotruncal) defects, hypocalcemia (no parathyroids).
  • Cri-du-chat: 5p deletion; cat-like cry, VSD. Williams: 7q11.23 (elastin); elfin face, hypercalcemia, very friendly, supravalvular aortic stenosis.
Q4. What is an isochromosome?
  • The centromere divides across (transversely) instead of lengthwise → one chromosome with two identical p arms and one with two identical q arms
  • Result: trisomy for one arm and monosomy for the other
  • Most common: i(Xq), a Turner syndrome variant. Less common: i(21q), i(9p), i(12p)
Step 1

i(12p) is the marker of testicular germ cell tumors.

Q5. What are inversions, and why do they matter only for offspring?
ParacentricPericentric
Definition2 breaks in one arm; segment flips; centromere not included2 breaks on either side of the centromere; segment with centromere flips (centromere position can change)
CarrierUsually healthy (balanced; nothing lost)
MeiosisHomologs form an inversion loop to pair
Crossover in loopDicentric and acentric chromosomes → nonviableDuplication/deletion (unbalanced) recombinants → affected offspring
Memory tool

PERIcentric = includes the centromere (peri = around it). PARAcentric = alongside, on one arm only.

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A child with Down syndrome has 46 chromosomes. Her healthy mother has 45. Explain.
Mother is a balanced Robertsonian carrier (e.g., 14;21); the child inherited the fused chromosome plus two normal 21s → translocation trisomy 21.
A2A couple has three miscarriages. The husband's karyotype is 46,XY,t(2;5)(q21;q31). Why the losses?
Adjacent segregation of his balanced reciprocal translocation gives unbalanced gametes (partial trisomy + partial monosomy), often lethal.
A3A woman with Turner features has 46 chromosomes: one normal X and one X with two long arms. Abnormality?
Isochromosome Xq, i(Xq): monosomy for Xp, trisomy for Xq.

LO 5Chromosomal mosaicism

Q1. What is mosaicism?

The presence, in one person or tissue, of at least two cell lines with different karyotypes, all derived from a single zygote. Example: 46,XX/47,XX,+21.

Trap

Mosaicism comes from one zygote. Two cell lines from two zygotes (fused twins) is chimerism.

Q2. How does mosaicism arise?
RouteStartEventResult
Mitotic nondisjunction (autosome)Normal 46 zygoteNondisjunction in an early mitosis → 47,+21 and 45,−21 cells; the monosomic line dies46/47,+21; mostly normal cells
Mitotic nondisjunction (sex chromosome)Normal 46,XX zygoteBoth products viable45,X / 46,XX / 47,XXX (three lines)
Meiotic nondisjunction + trisomy rescue47,+21 zygoteAnaphase lag: one extra 21 is lost in a later division46/47,+21; mostly abnormal cells
High yield

The earlier the error in development, the more tissues carry the abnormal line. Starting from a trisomic zygote leaves most cells abnormal.

Q3. What does mosaicism look like in a patient?
  • Usually a milder phenotype than the full trisomy
  • Uneven spread of abnormal cells → asymmetric body shape or appearance
  • Often hypo- or hyperpigmented skin patches
  • A normal blood karyotype doesn't rule it out; test another tissue (e.g., skin)
Step 1

Pigment streaks follow lines of Blaschko. Trisomy rescue can leave uniparental disomy (both copies of a chromosome from one parent) → imprinting disorders.

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1A girl has mild Down features and streaky skin pigmentation; her blood shows 46/47,+21 with 20% abnormal cells. Most likely mechanism?
Post-zygotic mitotic nondisjunction in a normal zygote → mostly normal cells, milder features.
A2A woman has 45,X/46,XX/47,XXX cells. How did three lines arise?
Mitotic nondisjunction of the X in a 46,XX embryo; both the 45,X and 47,XXX products survive.

LO 6Confined placental mosaicism

Q1. What is confined placental mosaicism (CPM)?
  • An abnormal (often trisomic) cell line found in the placenta but not the fetus
  • Detected in 1–2% of CVS samples (chorionic villus sampling tests placental tissue)
  • Possible patterns after an early error:
    • Mosaic in both placenta and fetus
    • Abnormal line only in the placenta (CPM)
    • Abnormal line only in the fetus
    • Placenta aneuploid, fetus normal (trisomy rescued in the fetal lineage)
Analogy — the packaging vs the product

CVS samples the box (placenta), not the product (fetus). A dented box doesn't mean a broken product, so an abnormal CVS result must be checked in fetal cells.

Q2. What do you do when CVS shows mosaicism?
  • Confirm in fetal cells with amniocentesis (amniotic fluid cells come from the fetus)
  • Detailed ultrasound for growth and anomalies
  • Counsel: CPM can still cause placental dysfunction / growth restriction, and a rescued fetus may have uniparental disomy
In-house exam

Know the number: CPM in 1–2% of CVS, and that it is a discrepancy between placenta and fetus.

ApplyLO 6 application questions

A1CVS at 11 weeks shows 46,XX/47,XX,+16 mosaicism. Ultrasound is normal. Next step?
Amniocentesis to karyotype fetal cells; this is likely confined placental mosaicism.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A newborn has Down syndrome. Karyotype is 47,XY,+21. What is the most likely mechanism?

≈95% of Down syndrome is meiotic nondisjunction, mostly maternal meiosis I, rising with maternal age.

2A child with Down syndrome has 46 chromosomes. The phenotypically normal mother has 45 chromosomes. What is the mother's karyotype most likely to show?

Balanced Robertsonian carriers have 45 chromosomes; unbalanced offspring have 46 with three copies of 21q.

3Which statement about whole-chromosome monosomy is correct?

Only 45,X is viable among full monosomies.

4Nondisjunction occurs in one meiotic division and produces two normal gametes, one with two identical copies of a chromosome and one with none. Which division failed?

A meiosis II error leaves half the gametes normal; the disomic gamete carries identical sister chromatids.

5A newborn has a cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia, omphalocele and a heart defect. Which karyotype is most likely?

Patau: midline defects (clefts, spina bifida, omphalocele), microphthalmia, heart defects.

6A 15-year-old girl has short stature, a webbed neck, a broad chest and no breast development. Which finding is expected?

Turner (45,X): proportionate short stature, ovarian dysgenesis, sexual infantilism, webbed neck, shield chest.

7Why are sex chromosome aneuploidies usually milder than autosomal ones?

Lyon hypothesis (X inactivation) plus the Y's <50 genes limit the dosage effect.

8A healthy man with recurrent pregnancy loss has 46 chromosomes with a segment of 2q exchanged for a segment of 7p. In meiosis, which segregation gives a normal or balanced gamete?

Alternate segregation → normal or balanced gametes; adjacent patterns → partial trisomy + partial monosomy.

9A deletion removes both ends of a chromosome, and the broken ends join. What forms?

Two breaks with loss of both termini and fusion of the centromeric segment = ring.

10A girl has mild Down features, asymmetric growth and streaky pigmentation. Blood karyotype: 46,XX[16]/47,XX,+21[4]. Best explanation?

Two cell lines from one zygote, mostly normal → mitotic nondisjunction; milder, asymmetric, pigment changes.

11CVS shows trisomy 2 in 30% of cells; amniocentesis shows a normal fetal karyotype. This is:

Abnormal line in the placenta only = CPM, found in 1–2% of CVS.

12A carrier of a pericentric inversion has a child with a duplication of one segment and a deletion of another on the same chromosome. How did this happen?

Crossover inside the inversion loop of a pericentric inversion → recombinant chromosomes with duplication/deletion. Paracentric crossovers make dicentric/acentric (nonviable) products.
